tagline: Follow the Columbia from western forests to eastern hills and desert.
intro: The Columbia River Gorge Scenic Byway follows SR 14 between Camas and Maryhill, with forests at its western end and rolling hills and desert country to the east. State of Washington Tourism presents the byway as a 90-mile, two-hour drive through the national scenic area, with overlooks and trails along the way. East of Washougal, SR 14 continues as a two-lane highway along the north side of the Columbia, opposite Oregon’s I-84.

The road began with a state survey in 1905 for a wagon route from Washougal to Lyle. Called the North Bank Highway, it was realigned closer to the Columbia in 1913 and extended west to Vancouver. US 830 joined its signs in 1926; the Evergreen Highway name followed in 1937. SR 14 is the later highway designation, covering a longer route than this scenic drive.

Heading east from Camas through Washougal, the highway passes Steigerwald Lake, Franz Lake and Pierce national wildlife refuges. Bonneville Dam and the Bridge of the Gods precede Stevenson. Beyond Stevenson, tunnels punctuate the river route before the White Salmon River crossing and Bingen. Continue across the Klickitat River into Lyle, then past Wishram toward Maryhill, where the museum and Stonehenge memorial mark the byway’s eastern end.

moments.title: Bridge of the Gods
moments.text: Bonneville Dam changed the dimensions of this crossing. The Wauna Toll Bridge Company opened the bridge in 1926, linking Cascade Locks with the Washington shore near Stevenson. Rising river levels required a 44-foot lift in 1938 and an extension from 1,127 feet to 1,858 feet. The Port of Cascade Locks bought the crossing in 1961. The steel truss cantilever span now carries the Pacific Crest Trail across the Columbia. In September 1927, onlookers saw Charles Lindbergh fly the Spirit of St. Louis over the new bridge, turn, and fly back beneath it.

moments.title: Bingen
moments.text: Bingen borrowed its name from Germany but gave it a different pronunciation. P.J. Suksdorf founded the town in 1892 and named it for Bingen am Rhein; here, the name is BIN-jen. Bingen incorporated in 1924, three decades after Suksdorf founded it. SR 14 follows the Columbia’s north bank through town, while SR 141 connects Bingen with White Salmon, Trout Lake and the base of Mount Adams. The Hood River Bridge lies west of town, linking the highway with Oregon. Bingen and neighboring White Salmon also have views across the river to Mount Hood.

moments.title: Maryhill
moments.text: Sam Hill’s planned Quaker community never materialized, but his Maryhill property became home to a concrete memorial to war’s dead. Hill commissioned the Stonehenge replica to commemorate Klickitat County’s World War I losses. He understood the ancient monument as a place of sacrifice and intended his version to express the needless sacrifice of modern warfare. Dedicated in 1918 and completed in 1929, the memorial overlooks the Columbia Gorge. The town’s buildings later burned, leaving the concrete replica standing. The memorial’s altar stone is aligned with sunrise at the summer solstice.
